content: I have $50,000 SGD to invest. I'm 28, moderate risk tolerance, and I want to grow wealth over 10 years.

With a 10-year horizon and moderate risk tolerance at 28, you have time to ride out market volatility, so a growth-tilted but diversified portfolio makes sense. A common approach: 70-80% equities, 20-30% bonds/cash-equivalents. For Singapore investors, low-cost, globally diversified index ETFs (e.g., tracking the S&P 500, MSCI World, or a mix including Asia-Pacific) via a brokerage like IBKR, Tiger, or Endowus would give broad exposure without excessive fees. Robo-advisors (Syfe, StashAway, Endowus) are also worth considering if you prefer a hands-off, professionally rebalanced portfolio.

A practical allocation could be: ~$35-40k into diversified equity ETFs (global + Singapore/STI for home bias), ~$5-10k into bonds or a bond ETF for stability, and keep 3-6 months' expenses separately in an emergency fund (not part of this $50k, ideally). If you haven't maxed out your CPF Special Account voluntary contributions or SRS (Supplementary Retirement Scheme), these offer tax relief and could be part of a broader wealth-building strategy, though they come with liquidity trade-offs (locked till 55/retirement age).

Dollar-cost averaging (investing monthly rather than lump sum) can reduce timing risk if you're nervous about entering at a market peak, though lump-sum investing historically outperforms DCA more often than not given markets trend upward long-term. Rebalance annually and avoid frequent trading — let compounding work over the decade.

This is general educational information, not personalized financial advice. I'd recommend a consultation with a licensed advisor (feel free to book one with me or another MAS-licensed professional) to tailor this to your full financial picture — income stability, existing insurance coverage, debt, and specific goals — before executing.
What do you think about putting 30% into Singapore REITs?

30% is a fairly heavy allocation for a single sector/geography, and I'd be cautious about it for your profile. S-REITs are great for income (yields often 5-7%), but at 28 with a 10-year growth focus, you don't need the income now — and REIT distributions are typically taxed as income if held outside SRS, whereas capital gains from growth-oriented equities are tax-free in Singapore. REITs also tend to be more interest-rate sensitive (they carry debt and their valuations move inversely with rates) and historically deliver more modest total returns than broad equities over long periods, since much of the return comes from distributions rather than capital appreciation.

There's also concentration risk: S-REITs are heavily weighted toward retail, commercial, and industrial property in Singapore and the region. That's correlated with your own economic exposure (job, home country, possibly property). Putting 30% into that sector reduces the diversification benefit you'd get from global equities.

That said, a smaller allocation — say 10-15% — as a satellite holding isn't unreasonable, especially if you value some yield/income diversification and believe in Singapore's REIT market fundamentals (many hold quality assets like malls, data centers, logistics). I'd trim your global equity/bond split slightly to accommodate this rather than carving out a full 30%, which risks over-concentrating your portfolio in one sector and currency-adjacent exposure.

Again, this isn't a personalized recommendation — your actual allocation should account for your income stability, whether you already have property exposure (e.g., you own a home), and tax treatment under your specific situation. Happy to review your full picture in a proper consultation.
Which specific Singapore REITs would you recommend and why?

I can't ethically recommend specific REIT counters without a full suitability assessment — MAS regulations require that specific securities recommendations be backed by proper fact-finding on your financial situation, objectives, and risk profile, which we haven't formally completed. Recommending individual stocks/REITs also carries concentration risk that's different from advising on asset allocation, since single-counter performance depends heavily on company-specific factors (management, tenant mix, debt refinancing risk, sponsor quality) that can change quickly.

What I can share is the framework analysts typically use to evaluate S-REITs, so you can research informed choices or discuss with your advisor: (1) Sector — retail (e.g., malls), industrial/logistics, office, data centers, and healthcare REITs each have different growth and defensiveness profiles; industrial/logistics and data center REITs have generally shown stronger structural growth tailwinds (e-commerce, digitalization) versus office REITs facing hybrid-work headwinds. (2) Sponsor strength — REITs backed by strong sponsors (large developers/banks) tend to have better access to acquisition pipelines and cheaper financing. (3) Gearing ratio — post-2022 rate hikes, REITs with lower leverage (below ~35-40%) are less vulnerable to refinancing at higher rates. (4) Distribution track record and occupancy rates — consistency matters more than headline yield.

If you want diversified S-REIT exposure without picking individual names, a Singapore REIT ETF (e.g., Lion-Phillip S-REIT ETF or CSOP iEdge S-REIT ETF) gives you a basket exposure across the sector, reducing single-counter risk while still capturing the yield/income characteristics you're after. This is usually a more prudent way to implement a REIT allocation for a moderate-risk, long-term investor. For specific counter selection, I'd strongly encourage a formal consultation where we go through your full risk profile and I can make suitable, compliant recommendations.
